card.summary: The only removal for the `.str` accessor in 3.1.0 is the kwargs catch-all on `Series.str.wrap`, so textwrap options must be passed as the named keyword arguments in its signature. Every other `Series.str` method remains, but the 3.1.0 signatures use explicit defaults (na=<no_default> on `Series.str.contains` and `Series.str.startswith`, regex=False on `Series.str.replace`, regex=None on `Series.str.split`), so code should pass these keywords explicitly instead of relying on old implicit behaviour.

traps.trap: Passing arbitrary extra keyword arguments through `Series.str.wrap` to textwrap, relying on its old kwargs catch-all.
traps.instead: Pass only the named parameters listed in the `Series.str.wrap` signature (width, break_long_words, max_lines, placeholder and the others). Any other keyword fails because the kwargs parameter is removed.

traps.trap: Calling `Series.str.replace` with a regex pattern and expecting it to be treated as a regex by default.
traps.instead: Pass regex=True whenever pat is a regular expression. With the default regex=False, pat is matched as a literal string, so '.' only replaces a real dot.
traps.evidence: case: 'bool | None' = None, flags: 'int' = 0, regex: 'bool' = False

traps.trap: Using the mask from `Series.str.contains` on data with missing values without setting na, then indexing with it.
traps.instead: Pass na=False (or na=True) explicitly so the result is a plain boolean mask that is safe to use for filtering.

traps.trap: Assuming `Series.str.startswith` and `Series.str.endswith` return NaN for missing values and accept only a single prefix.
traps.instead: Pass na=False explicitly for a clean boolean mask. To test several prefixes or suffixes, pass a tuple of strings.

traps.trap: Calling `Series.str.split` with a multi-character regex pattern and leaving the regex keyword unset.
traps.instead: Pass regex=True for a regex pattern, or regex=False for a literal separator, so the result does not depend on how pandas guesses from the pattern.

traps.trap: Using `Series.str.match` to validate that a whole string fits a pattern.
traps.instead: Use `Series.str.fullmatch` to check the whole string. `Series.str.match` is anchored only at the start, so trailing characters still match.
traps.evidence: Determine if each string starts with a match of a regular expression.

traps.trap: Calling `Series.str.cat` on Series with different indexes and expecting a positional concatenation without missing parts.
traps.instead: Remember that others are aligned on the index with a left join. Pass join explicitly, and pass na_rep so unmatched rows are not turned into missing values.

example.explains: Uses explicit regex, na and join keywords and named wrap parameters, which is the 3.1.0-safe way to call the `.str` accessor.
example.code:
import pandas as pd

# replace: pass regex=True for a regex; the default is a literal match
s = pd.Series(["apple pie", "Banana-split", "cherry tart"])
r = s.str.replace(r"[-\s]+", "_", regex=True)
assert r.tolist() == ["apple_pie", "Banana_split", "cherry_tart"]
lit = pd.Series(["a.b", "axb"]).str.replace(".", "-")
assert lit.tolist() == ["a-b", "axb"]

# contains / startswith: give na explicitly for a clean boolean mask
m = pd.Series(["apple", "Banana", None, "cherry"])
mask = m.str.contains("an", case=False, na=False)
assert mask.tolist() == [False, True, False, False]
starts = m.str.startswith(("apple", "cherry"), na=False)
assert starts.tolist() == [True, False, False, True]

# match is anchored at the start only; fullmatch checks the whole string
d = pd.Series(["2024-01-05", "2024-01-05x"])
assert d.str.match(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}").tolist() == [True, True]
assert d.str.fullmatch(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}").tolist() == [True, False]

# split: say whether the pattern is a regex
parts = pd.Series(["a1b22c"]).str.split(r"\d+", regex=True, expand=True)
assert parts.iloc[0].tolist() == ["a", "b", "c"]

# wrap: only the named textwrap parameters are accepted (no extra kwargs)
w = pd.Series(["the quick brown fox"]).str.wrap(width=10, break_long_words=False)
assert w.iloc[0] == "the quick\nbrown fox"

# cat aligns on the index; set join and na_rep explicitly
left = pd.Series(["a", "b"], index=[0, 1])
right = pd.Series(["x", "y"], index=[1, 2])
c = left.str.cat(right, sep="-", na_rep="?", join="left")
assert c.tolist() == ["a-?", "b-x"]
print("ok")

card.summary: Between 2.3.3 and 3.1.0 the only recorded change to the `.str` accessor is the removal of the kwargs catch-all from `Series.str.wrap`; no `Series.str` method was removed. Textwrap options must now be passed as the named keywords in the `Series.str.wrap` signature, and the other `Series.str` methods keep the signatures listed in the catalogue.

traps.trap: Passing arbitrary extra keyword arguments through `Series.str.wrap` to textwrap, relying on its old kwargs catch-all.
traps.instead: Pass only the named parameters in the `Series.str.wrap` signature, such as width, break_long_words, max_lines and placeholder. The kwargs parameter is removed in 3.1.0.

traps.trap: Passing a regular expression to `Series.str.replace` without setting regex, expecting it to be treated as a regex.
traps.instead: Pass regex=True when pat is a regular expression and regex=False when it is a literal string. The signature default is regex=False.
traps.evidence: case: 'bool | None' = None, flags: 'int' = 0, regex: 'bool' = False

traps.trap: Leaving na unset in `Series.str.contains` on data with missing values and then filtering with the result.
traps.instead: Pass na=False (or na=True) so your code sets the result for missing entries. The default is the <no_default> sentinel, and the catalogue does not say what it resolves to.

traps.trap: Combining several `Series.str.startswith` or `Series.str.endswith` calls with | to test more than one prefix or suffix.
traps.instead: Pass a tuple of strings as pat in a single call, which the signature accepts. Pass na explicitly as well.

traps.trap: Using `Series.str.match` to check that a whole string fits a pattern.
traps.instead: Use `Series.str.fullmatch` for whole-string checks. `Series.str.match` only requires a match at the start, so trailing characters still pass.
traps.evidence: Determine if each string starts with a match of a regular expression.

traps.trap: Calling `Series.str.cat` with another Series that has a different index and expecting a purely positional concatenation.
traps.instead: Remember that others are aligned using join, which defaults to 'left'. Pass join explicitly, and pass na_rep to set the text used for missing parts.
